Customer narratives: Day 0, Day 1 and Day N

Most specifications describe the user who has nothing. Most users have something. The gap between those two sentences is where launches go wrong.

1 · The draftA five-page solution section that described one user in twenty

On the morning of 9 February 2026, Ritu Varadarajan read the same document for the third time in a week and still could not name what was missing from it. She was the group product manager for savings at Divyakosh Money, a Pune-based consumer investing app that had been distributing mutual funds as an AMFI-registered distributor since 2019. The company had 2.8 million registered users, of whom 640,000 were monthly active investors, and roughly ₹2,900 crore of client assets under advice. Ritu had nine engineers, eleven weeks, and a launch date of 6 April.

The document was the product requirements document — the PRD, the written specification a team agrees on before it builds — for a feature called Goals. The idea was straightforward. Instead of asking a customer to choose a mutual fund, Divyakosh would ask what the money was for, and work backwards to a monthly contribution. The solution section ran five pages and was written, as her team had been taught to write, as a story about a person.

The story was about Priya, twenty-nine, a systems analyst in Hyderabad. Priya opens the app, taps the new Goals tab, chooses Emergency fund from six templates, types ₹3,00,000 and eighteen months, watches the app propose ₹15,800 a month into a liquid fund, and confirms. A systematic investment plan — an SIP, a standing instruction that moves a fixed sum from her bank account into a fund on the same date every month — begins on the first of the following month. It was a good story. Ritu had read it aloud in a review and people had nodded.

What she finally saw on the third reading was an arithmetic problem hiding inside a narrative one. Priya had no investments. Of the 640,000 people who would be active on Divyakosh in April, about 38,000 would be new that month. The other 602,000 had been there for a while, and 62 per cent of those — 373,240 people — had at least one SIP already running, an average of 2.4 each. On the morning of 6 April, every one of them would open the app and find a Goals tab. The PRD did not say what was in it.

Nor did it say what the tab looked like in June 2027, when a person who started four goals had met one, abandoned two, and was still receiving a monthly nudge about a wedding that had already happened. The specification described the first ninety seconds of a product that people would live inside for years.

2 · The ideaThree narratives, not one

A customer narrative is a short account, written as prose in the order things happen, of one specified person using the product: what they already have, what causes them to arrive, what they see on the screen, what they do, and what changes as a result. It is not a list of requirements. It is the requirements told as a scene, so that anything the team has failed to decide shows up as a sentence nobody can write.

The Day 0 / Day N discipline is the rule that a feature is not specified until it has been written at least three times, for three different populations:

Day 0 — the greenfield narrative. A person meeting the product and the feature together for the first time. They have no data, no settings, no history, and no habits. Everything they see, the product must explain.

Day 1 — the brownfield narrative. A person who already uses the product, meeting the feature for the first time. The terms are borrowed from construction: greenfield is an empty site, brownfield is a site with something already standing on it that you must either work around or demolish. This person has data that predates the feature, preferences they set eighteen months ago, and a mental model of what the app does, into which the new thing must be inserted without breaking anything.

Day N — the steady-state narrative. The same person much later, when the feature has accumulated history. Things have piled up. The explanatory tooltips have been dismissed. Some of what they created is stale, some is finished, and some was a mistake. The product's job on Day N is not to teach; it is to stay legible under weight.

The lineage is older than software product management. Scenario-based design was formalised by John M. Carroll and colleagues at IBM's Watson centre through the late 1980s and set out at length in his Making Use (2000); Alan Cooper's The Inmates Are Running the Asylum (1999) pushed the same instinct into personas and goal-directed design; Amazon's internal habit of writing the press release and customer FAQ before the code, widely reported from the early 2000s, is the same move made at the level of a whole product. The specific Day 0 / Day 1 / Day N triple is folk craft rather than any one author's framework — it circulates in engineering teams because migration incidents teach it. That is worth saying plainly: nobody owns it, and you should not cite it as though somebody did.

The sentence Ritu could say in a room without sounding glib: “We have written this feature once, for the person who has nothing. Nineteen in twenty of the people who will see it in April already have something.”

3 · The mechanicsWhat each narrative must name, including the parts left implicit

Writing a narrative well is mostly a matter of refusing to be vague at six specific places. Practitioners who have been burned tend to fill in all six without thinking about it; newcomers fill in two and assume the rest.

The actor and the inventory. Not “the user” but a person with a stated holding: Sandhya, 34, Coimbatore, three running SIPs totalling ₹10,000 a month, joined in 2022, has never opened the fund-detail screen. The inventory is the part people skip, and it is the part that produces requirements. A person with three SIPs needs a mapping rule. A person with none does not.

The trigger. What put them on this screen. A push notification, a bank debit alert, a colleague's remark, a tab that appeared overnight. Day 1 narratives almost always have a trigger the team controls — the announcement — and teams almost always forget it is part of the feature.

What they see, in the words on the screen. Narratives that say “the user is shown their goals” hide the decision. Narratives that quote the empty-state line — “No goals yet” — surface it.

The state change. What is different in the system afterwards, named as data: a goal row created, three SIPs linked, a reminder schedule started.

The migration rule and its default (Day 1 only). Automatic or proposed? Reversible or not? What happens to the person for whom the rule guesses wrong? At Divyakosh the rule was a classifier over fund category, SIP size and tenure, and its accuracy on a hand-labelled sample of 400 accounts was 92 per cent. Eight per cent wrong, applied silently, is the difference between a feature and an incident.

The accumulation variable (Day N only). What grows, and how fast. For Goals it was the number of goals per user (1.0 at creation, 2.3 by month twelve) and the share of them dormant. A Day N narrative without a number in it is not a Day N narrative; it is the Day 1 narrative with the word “later” added.

Two further steps are almost always implicit and should not be. The first is the reversal narrative: the person turns the feature off, deletes the goal, or leaves. At Divyakosh this mattered acutely, because a goal was a label on top of a real financial instrument; deleting the label must not stop the SIP, and the screen had to say so. The second is attaching each narrative to acceptance criteria and telemetry — the pass/fail conditions a tester checks, and the events that let you see afterwards whether the story actually happened. A narrative that nobody can falsify after launch is a piece of writing, not a specification.

4 · The arithmeticWho actually meets the feature, and what an error costs

Ritu's argument in the 12 February review was not aesthetic. She built a table of how many people would live each narrative, and what one percentage point of defect would cost in each.

Base: 640,000 monthly active investors at launch; 602,000 of them pre-existing; 62 per cent of pre-existing actives hold at least one SIP. Month-12 Day N figure assumes 46 per cent adoption of Goals across a base that has grown to roughly 933,000 actives, and that 61 per cent of adopters have held a goal for six months or more.

Read line by line, the table says something the PRD had obscured. In the launch month, the brownfield population with SIPs is 9.8 times the greenfield population. A defect in the greenfield path spreads thinly across a month and lands on people who have invested nothing. A defect in the brownfield mapping lands inside seventy-two hours, concentrated, on the customers with money in the product — and it lands as a wrong statement about their own finances, which is the category of error that produces screenshots on social media rather than support tickets.

Now run the arithmetic on the migration rule. The classifier is 92 per cent accurate on a 400-account sample. Applied automatically to 373,240 accounts, it mislabels roughly 29,859 of them. Of those, Divyakosh's own historical rate of confusion-to-contact — the share of confused users who write in — was 18 per cent, giving about 5,375 conversations in the first week. The support team handled 1,900 conversations a week.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose the growth team's April campaign triples new sign-ups, to 114,000 in month 1. The Day 0 exposure per point of defect rises to 1,140 people — but the brownfield exposure is unchanged at 3,732, so the ratio only falls from 9.8 to 3.3. The conclusion survives a threefold change in the input that most obviously threatens it, which is what makes it worth acting on.

Now change a different input. Suppose the team abandons automatic mapping and simply shows existing users the Day 0 empty state — the cheap option, and the one most teams take by default because it requires no decision. The defect rate is now zero by construction: nothing is mislabelled. But 373,240 people with live SIPs are told “No goals yet. Tell us what the money is for.” No test suite catches this, because nothing is broken. Applying the same 18 per cent contact rate to even a conservative 3 per cent confusion rate gives 2,015 conversations — still above a week's capacity, and generated by a screen that passed every acceptance test written for it.

5 · NuancesThe distinctions that separate practitioners from vocabulary

Day N is a quantity, not a date

“Day N” sounds temporal and is not. What makes the late state different is accumulation: number of goals, number of records, number of teammates, number of dismissed notifications. If a product's accumulation variable stays flat — a one-shot tax-filing flow, say — then Day N is Day 1 and you should say so rather than inventing a narrative. Conversely, a product whose data grows fast can reach Day N in a fortnight. The right question is never “what does this look like in a year” but “what does this look like at 200 of them.”

Day 0 for the person is not Day 0 for the account

In business software the two come apart constantly. When Divyansh Field Cloud, a Bengaluru company selling job-scheduling software to appliance-service networks, adds a technician to a customer with four years of history, that technician is at Day 0 personally and Day N organisationally: everything is new to her, and nothing is empty. This population — new person, old account — is the single most reliably under-specified group in B2B products, because the onboarding flow was built for the founding admin.

The migration default is the loudest requirement in the document

Whatever the brownfield rule does by default is what happens to almost everyone, because almost nobody changes a default. That makes the default a product decision of the first order, and it is routinely made implicitly, late, by an engineer writing a data-backfill script under time pressure. The tell is a PRD in which the word “migration” appears only in the engineering section.

Narratives are not user stories, use cases or journey maps

A user story is a one-line placeholder for a conversation (“as an investor I want to name my savings so that I can track them”); it is a unit of planning, and deliberately holds no detail. A use case, in the formal sense Ivar Jacobson gave it in the 1990s, enumerates a main flow and every alternate and exception flow — it is more complete than a narrative and much less readable, and it describes the system's behaviour rather than the person's experience. A journey map spans channels and time across a whole relationship, usually without any particular feature in it. A customer narrative sits between them: one person, one feature, one sitting, told as prose. Narratives are journey maps with the new feature inserted, cut down to the length people will actually read.

Empty state, zero state and error state are three different screens

The screen for “you have not created anything yet” teaches. The screen for “you had things and now the filter matches none of them” must offer to clear the filter. The screen for “we could not load your things” must offer to retry and must never say “No goals yet,” because telling an investor their goals do not exist when the server is down is a distinct and much worse failure. Teams that write only the Day 0 narrative typically ship one screen for all three.

A narrative you cannot falsify is a slogan

Test each sentence by asking whether it could be untrue of a real person. “Priya wants to feel in control of her finances” cannot be false and therefore constrains nothing. “Priya has ₹41,000 in a liquid fund and a bank balance that drops below ₹5,000 on the 28th of most months” can be checked, and it generates requirements about when to schedule the debit.

Narratives specify shape, not demand

This is the limit worth internalising. Three beautifully written narratives tell you exactly what to build and nothing whatsoever about whether anyone wants it, how often they would return, or what they would pay. Narratives are a specification instrument, not a discovery instrument. Teams that mistake a vivid story for evidence of demand build well-specified products nobody opens.

The exit narrative is always missing

Ask what happens when the person deletes, disables, downgrades or dies. At Divyakosh, deleting a goal must not cancel the underlying SIP, and the confirmation dialogue must say which of the two is happening. In B2B the equivalent is the departing employee whose records must be reassigned. The exit narrative is where data-protection obligations under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 usually first become concrete for a product team.

6 · Across product types and stages

In consumer products the Day 0 narrative carries unusual weight because acquisition is continuous and unforgiving: a meaningful share of the audience is always new, and the first session decides retention. But the brownfield spike is still the larger single event, as Exhibit 1 shows, and consumer teams under-invest in it precisely because their instincts are tuned to acquisition.

In B2B and enterprise products the weighting inverts. New logos arrive a few a week; the installed base is the product. Here Day 1 is not one narrative but three, because an account has roles: the administrator who must decide whether to enable the feature, the manager whose reports change shape, and the frontline user who was not consulted. A feature that is delightful for the frontline user and invisible to the administrator does not get switched on. Divyansh Field Cloud learned this when a scheduling change that tested beautifully with technicians sat at 4 per cent enablement for two quarters because no narrative had ever been written for the operations head who owned the setting.

In marketplaces every narrative doubles, because there are two populations whose Day 0s are asymmetric. At Divyaneel Bazaar, a Bengaluru platform connecting apparel manufacturers in Tiruppur with multi-brand retail stores, a buyer's Day 0 is empty of the buyer's own data but full of supply; a seller's Day 0 is empty of demand and stays empty until the platform routes some. Writing a seller Day 0 narrative that quietly assumes orders already exist is the most common specification error in marketplace products.

By stage, the difference is real and often stated backwards. An early company has almost no brownfield — with 4,000 users you can email all of them, and the migration is cheap — so Day 0 genuinely dominates. A large company's centre of gravity is Day 1 and Day N, and the expensive mistake is to keep specifying like a startup long after the installed base has become the business. Divyakosh crossed that line somewhere around 2024 and its PRD template had not noticed.

7 · Common mistakes

Specifying only the greenfield story

Symptom from outside: the launch demo is beautiful and the week-one support queue is full of tenured customers asking what happened to their account. Underlying misunderstanding: confusing the story that sells the feature internally with the story that specifies it. Cheapest diagnostic: compute the ratio in Exhibit 1 — what share of month-one exposure is new users? It takes twenty minutes and settles the argument.

Treating migration as an engineering task

Symptom: the migration default is decided in a stand-up within a week of launch, verbally. Misunderstanding: that moving data and deciding what the customer sees are the same activity. Diagnostic: ask three people on the team to write, separately and in one sentence, what an existing customer sees on the morning of launch. If the three sentences differ, the requirement does not exist.

A Day N narrative with no number in it

Symptom: the Day N section reads like the Day 1 section with “over time” inserted. Misunderstanding: that Day N is about elapsed time rather than accumulated volume. Diagnostic: ask what grows, at what rate, and what the screen looks like at ten times the current value. If nobody can name the growing quantity, there is no Day N specification.

Actors without inventories

Symptom: narratives that begin “the user wants to…” Misunderstanding: that a narrative is about motivation. Diagnostic: underline every noun naming something the person already possesses — data, settings, habits, colleagues, money. If there are no underlines, you are reading marketing copy.

8 · What good looks like

A well-handled version of Ritu's decision is not more elaborate; it is differently ordered. The solution section opens with a one-paragraph statement of the three populations and their sizes, so that the reader knows before reading any story how much each one matters. Then three narratives, each roughly 250 words, each naming an actor with an inventory, a trigger, the words on the screen, the state change, and — for Day 1 — the migration rule with its accuracy and its reversal path, and — for Day N — the accumulation variable with a number. A fourth, shorter narrative covers exit. Each narrative is followed by its acceptance criteria and the two or three telemetry events that will let the team check, six weeks later, whether the story actually happened. The document is not longer than the one it replaces; the five pages spent on Priya become two, and the other three go where the people are.

9 · The decisionWhat Ritu did, and what to read next

On 16 February, Ritu re-cut the PRD and made three changes she could defend with the table rather than with taste. First, the brownfield path became the priority-zero scope: at launch, an existing investor with running SIPs would see a proposal — “we think these three SIPs are for these goals” — with a single confirm action and a visible way to change any row. Nothing would be filed silently, which converted a 92-per-cent-accurate classifier from a liability into a helpful first draft. Second, the dormancy rule was specified before launch rather than after: a goal with no contribution for ninety days would be marked dormant, drop out of the reminder schedule, and offer two actions, resume or archive. Third, to pay for both, she cut the six goal templates to two and dropped a projection chart, and moved the date from 6 April to 20 April.

The reasoning she gave the leadership team was the sentence she had been unable to say a week earlier: the feature had been designed for 38,000 people and would be met by 602,000, and the cheapest fix available was to write two more stories before writing any more code.

What to learn next follows directly. Acceptance criteria and error cases turn each narrative into something testable, which is the step that stops narratives becoming decoration. Telemetry requirements let you find out afterwards which of your three stories was true. And PRD structure is the container: narratives are the solution section, and a PRD whose template has one narrative slot will keep producing one-narrative products no matter how well its authors understand this page.

Two questions to sit with. First: for a feature you shipped in the last year, what fraction of the people who met it in the first month were new to the product — and did your specification reflect that fraction? Second: what is the accumulation variable in your product, what is its value at the ninetieth percentile of your users today, and when did you last look at a screen with that much on it?

Layakam Health: Writing the Refill Plan Narratives

A teaching case on customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N)

1. Opening

At 5:00 pm on Thursday 29 October 2026, Vyshali Elayidom closed a meeting-room door at Infopark, Kochi, and dialled in three colleagues: Vishwesh Eranholi in Pune, Vineela Edavalath in Singapore, where it was 7:30 pm, and Vyshnav Elankath in Berlin, where the clocks had gone back four days earlier and it was 12:30 pm. As Head of Product at Layakam Health, she owed engineering a decision by 10:00 am IST on Monday 2 November, when planning for sprint 47 would lock.

The feature was Refill Plan, which would reorder a patient's monthly medicines automatically. Building it was settled. Open was which stories the requirements should be written from: the first-time user's, the existing user's, and that of the day, weeks later, when the first automatic refill came due.

2. Company background

Layakam Health was founded in Kochi in March 2022 to manage repeat medicines for people with diabetes, hypertension and thyroid conditions. A customer uploads a prescription, Layakam's pharmacists verify it, and one of 1,400 partner pharmacies in Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu delivers. Schedule H medicines may be dispensed only against a prescription, and Layakam's house policy treats a prescription as valid for refills for six months.

In FY 2025-26 (April 2025 to March 2026) Layakam processed orders worth ₹96 crore. On 25 October 2026 it had 2,10,000 registered users, of whom 64,000 had ordered chronic medicines at least twice in the preceding 90 days, and it was adding about 9,000 users a month (August to October average). Rivals Tata 1mg, PharmEasy and Apollo 24/7 are far larger. Refill Plan would charge through UPI AutoPay, and the RBI's e-mandate framework requires a pre-debit notification at least 24 hours before every debit.

3. The situation

A customer approves a UPI AutoPay mandate once. The app then places the next order 28 days after the last, for a 30-day supply, after sending the pre-debit notice. Between Monday 7 and Sunday 13 September 2026, Vyshali's team piloted a prototype with 1,200 new users and 800 existing repeat-chronic users. First refills fell due 28 days after enrolment, between 5 and 11 October, so every Day 30 outcome had closed by 13 October, the day before the data was pulled. Exhibit 1 sets out the three scenarios and Exhibit 2 reports the pilot.

In the pilot, 62.0 per cent of invited new users and 38.0 per cent of invited existing users approved a mandate. Of those, 612 new and 228 existing users received a first automatic refill. The remaining 132 and 76 did not, for the three reasons in Exhibit 2, and Vineela's team phoned each of them. She costs a rescued refill at ₹310: ₹150 of agent time and ₹160 for a second delivery attempt.

Vishwesh's email of Wednesday 28 October estimated the build at 30 engineer-days for the new-user path, 14 for the existing-user path and 16 for the Day N path. Six engineers were free for sprint 47. Diwali falls on Sunday 8 November and the company closes on Monday 9 and Tuesday 10, leaving eight working days (2 to 6 and 11 to 13 November), or 48 engineer-days. A week of regression testing follows the build, so work finished by Friday 13 November could reach customers on Monday 23 November. A customer enrolling that day would reach Day 28 on Monday 21 December, when Vineela's team runs at about half strength for year-end leave (Figure 1).

Outside counsel had also been asked whether saved prescriptions could be reused for automatic refills under the DPDP Act. Written advice was due Monday 14 December.

4. The people

Vyshali Elayidom, Head of Product, Kochi. She joined in April 2024 and owns the decision. She wants requirements that engineers can build from without asking what the customer sees.

Vishwesh Eranholi, Engineering Lead, Pune. At Layakam since August 2022, he leads the six engineers on the feature. He wants one tightly scoped narrative the team can finish inside the sprint, and distrusts estimates for work nobody has specified.

Vineela Edavalath, Head of Customer Success, Singapore. She joined in January 2023 and runs a team of 14. Many callers are adult children abroad paying for a parent's medicines in Kerala. She wants the app to handle the weeks after enrolment so her agents are not the safety net.

Vyshnav Elankath, Senior Designer, Berlin. Joined in November 2024. He wants the home screen to treat a customer of two years and one of two minutes differently, and says a design built for one will confuse the other.

6. The options

Option A: Day 0 for new users only. Vyshali would write one narrative, from install to first scheduled order. It needs 30 engineer-days and leaves 18 spare in the sprint, at a build cost of ₹3.45 lakh, with release on Monday 23 November. Existing users would not see Refill Plan and no Day N states would be built. Exhibit 3 puts the failures Vineela's team would carry at 990 cases and ₹3.07 lakh for each month of sign-ups.

Option B: all three narratives. It writes all three stories before the build starts. It needs 60 engineer-days against 48, so two days of work move into sprint 48 and release moves to Wednesday 25 November, at ₹6.90 lakh. All 64,000 repeat-chronic users could be offered Refill Plan 19 days before counsel's advice is due.

Option C: Day 0 and Day N for new users. It needs 46 engineer-days, leaving two spare, at ₹5.29 lakh, with release on Monday 23 November. On Vineela's estimate rescue cases fall to 330 a month, or ₹1.02 lakh. Existing users would not see Refill Plan at release and no existing-user narrative would be written in this sprint.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 1 lists three scenarios. For each, what does Layakam know from the pilot, and what must it assume?
  2. Take each reason in the "not executed" rows of Exhibit 2. At what point in a customer's story does it occur, and what would a narrative have to show for a requirement to exist?
  3. Which options in Exhibit 3 fit inside sprint 47's 48 engineer-days, and which scenarios does each leave without a written narrative?
  4. Vyshali must name one option on Monday 2 November. Which would you put forward, and which single figure in the exhibits, if wrong, would change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

A narrative tells the feature's story for one person at one moment, and each scenario yields requirements that another cannot. The first-time user needs an enrolment path. The existing user needs a path that deals with what the app already holds about them. The user on Day N needs the states that exist only weeks after enrolment. A well-reasoned answer ties each narrative to evidence, counts the capacity left, and dates each unwritten narrative.

One defensible path is Option C. For new users the pilot gives direct evidence at both ends: 744 enrolments, and 132 refills that failed when due. Building Day N inside sprint 47 leaves two engineer-days of slack, and 21 December falls where agent cover is thinnest. The existing-user narrative is deferred with a date rather than dropped. It would be written in January, after counsel's advice of 14 December and an audit of how many saved prescriptions are older than six months, a reason behind 38 of the 76 existing-user failures. The path would change if the two-thirds estimate proved weak or if counsel cleared reuse early.

Delivery & Technology · Requirements & Specification

Customer narratives in depth: Day 0, Day 1, Day N and Day R

A feature is not one product. It is at least four, distinguished not by time but by what the person already has when they meet it — and most specifications describe only the emptiest of the four.

1 · Two rooms, one problem

On 3 March 2026, Anand Krishnamoorthy sat in a fourth-floor conference room on Mount Road in Chennai with a printout he had annotated in two colours. He was VP of Product at Diptanshu Care Systems, which had built clinical information software since 2016 and now ran in 34 hospitals across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Telangana — 11,400 beds, about 9,200 clinicians logging in during any given week. The feature in front of him was the largest thing the company had attempted: a drafting assistant that read an inpatient encounter record and produced the discharge summary that a doctor would review and sign.

The specification described a resident in general medicine finishing a round, opening a discharge, and finding a draft already written. It was accurate and it was useless, because Diptanshu's database held 641 distinct discharge-summary templates, accumulated over nine years by 34 hospitals, some of them NABH-accredited and holding template language their accreditation assessors had approved. The question the document did not answer was what happened to those 641 templates on the morning the assistant switched on. The second question it did not answer was what a discharge summary looked like in month fourteen, when the resident had signed nine hundred drafts and had long since stopped reading them closely.

Fifteen days earlier and 340 kilometres away, Simran Kaur Ahluwalia had been looking at a different version of the same hole. She was Director of Product at Divyanka Bazaar, a Bengaluru business-to-business marketplace founded in 2021 that connected apparel manufacturers in Tiruppur and Ludhiana with multi-brand retail stores in Tier-2 India. Divyanka had 4,100 sellers who had transacted in the last quarter, about 27,000 buying stores, and annualised gross merchandise value of roughly ₹1,180 crore. The feature was Standing Orders: a buyer could set a recurring replenishment — sixty pieces of a given style every fortnight — and a seller would see committed demand instead of a stream of surprises.

Her specification, too, told one story: a store owner in Hubballi who had bought the same kurta six times and now clicked “make this recurring.” It said nothing about the seller in Tiruppur who had never had a standing order and therefore had nothing on the new Standing Orders screen — the screen that was supposed to sell him on committing capacity. On a marketplace, the emptiest narrative is not the newest user. It is the side of the market the product has not yet fed.

The two situations differ in every visible respect: one is regulated enterprise healthcare with clinical liability, the other a two-sided commercial marketplace with no liability more serious than a missed delivery. They fail in the same way, and the failure has a name.

2 · The idea, and who disagrees about it

A customer narrative is a short prose account of one specified person using the product in one sitting, written in the order events occur, stating what that person already possesses, what brought them to the screen, what words they see, what they do, and what changes in the system as a result. The Day 0 / Day N discipline holds that a feature is not specified until the narrative has been written separately for each population that differs in what it possesses.

The conventional triple is Day 0 (greenfield — nothing pre-exists), Day 1 (brownfield — the product's existing state pre-exists but the feature's does not), and Day N (steady state — the feature's own state has accumulated). The triple is incomplete in a way that matters, and the fourth cell is best seen on a grid.

The intellectual history runs through three traditions that were never reconciled. Scenario-based design was formalised by John M. Carroll and colleagues at IBM's Watson research centre through the late 1980s and set out at length in Making Use (2000); its claim is that concrete scenarios, not abstract requirements, are the right medium for design reasoning, because abstraction hides exactly the situational detail on which usability turns. Goal-directed design, as Alan Cooper argued in The Inmates Are Running the Asylum (1999), added personas — fictional but evidence-grounded actors — to stop scenarios drifting toward whoever was in the room. Use-case analysis, from Ivar Jacobson's object-oriented work in the 1990s and given its practical form in Alistair Cockburn's Writing Effective Use Cases (2001), came from the opposite direction: enumerate the main flow and every alternate and exception flow until the behaviour is closed. Amazon's practice of writing a press release and customer FAQ before building, widely reported from the early 2000s, applies narrative at the level of a whole product rather than a feature.

These traditions disagree, and the disagreements are load-bearing rather than semantic.

The narrative-first school would sign the proposition that a specification whose scenarios are vivid and specific will generate the right requirements as a by-product. It would not sign the proposition that a narrative is sufficient assurance for a safety-relevant flow. The enumeration school signs the reverse: only a closed enumeration of flows can be tested for completeness, but not a reader can understand a forty-page use-case document well enough to notice what is missing. Anand's situation sits exactly on this fault line: a discharge summary is a legal clinical document, and a lyrical scenario about a resident on a round is not an adequate account of what happens when the draft is wrong.

A third position, from the jobs-to-be-done tradition — Anthony Ulwick's outcome-driven work from the 1990s and Clayton Christensen's later popularisation — is sceptical of narratives altogether. It signs specify the outcome the customer is hiring the product for, and the metrics by which they judge it, and refuses specify a persona's morning, on the grounds that narratives over-fit to incidental circumstance and smuggle in solution assumptions. Jeff Patton's story-mapping school (User Story Mapping, 2014) signs a fourth thing: that the unit of specification is a thin slice across an entire journey, and that Day 0 / Day N is really an argument about which slices you cut.

The sharpest live disagreement, and the one this page will not resolve, is whether Day N belongs in a specification at all. One camp holds that steady-state behaviour is unknowable before launch and that writing it early produces confident fiction. The other holds that the steady state is where the product spends ninety per cent of its life, and that leaving it to a later “polish” epic is how products become unusable at exactly the moment they become successful. Both have evidence. Section 10 returns to it.

Beyond the six slots sit four second-order effects that separate a competent specification from an expert one.

The default is the policy. Whatever the brownfield rule does without being asked is what happens to nearly the whole population, because defaults are almost never changed. This converts a data-migration decision into a policy decision with distributional consequences, and it is routinely made implicitly and late, by whoever writes the backfill.

The announcement is part of the feature. Day 1 has a trigger the company controls, and the in-product message, the email and the release note determine what fraction of the population even enters the narrative. Treating these as marketing artefacts produced after code freeze severs the specification from the only lever that decides its reach.

Reversibility substitutes for accuracy. Teams argue about whether a migration classifier is 88 or 93 per cent accurate when the decision that actually matters is what happens to the people it gets wrong. This is a design variable with four rungs, and choosing a lower rung buys you the right to be less accurate.

Trust decays, and Day N is where it decays to. This is the second-order effect that most often goes unspecified, and in AI-assisted products it is quantifiable. Diptanshu ran a fourteen-hospital pilot from October 2025. The measured draft error rate — drafts containing at least one clinically material inaccuracy, adjudicated by a review panel — was stable at about 6 per cent across the pilot. What moved was the clinician. In week 1, 71 per cent of drafts were materially edited before signature and the panel judged that clinicians caught 88 per cent of the material errors. By week 30, the edit rate had fallen to 22 per cent and the catch rate to 41 per cent.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. Per 1,000 discharges there are 60 erroneous drafts. At an 88 per cent catch rate, 7.2 errors reach a signed document. At 41 per cent, 35.4 do. The model did not get worse. The product got worse, at a rate of roughly one additional escaped error per 1,000 discharges per month, and no Day 0 narrative can see this because it is a property of the hundredth encounter, not the first.

4 · When the discipline applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as claims you can test on a specific feature rather than as advice.

Claim 1: a population exists that holds state the feature touches. True at Diptanshu — 641 templates, plus every unsigned draft in flight at cutover. True at Divyanka — 27,000 buyers with order history from which standing orders can be inferred. Where this claim is false, Day 1 collapses into Day 0 and you should say so in one sentence rather than write a ceremonial narrative.

Claim 2: the accumulation variable grows materially within the horizon. At Diptanshu, signed drafts per clinician reach roughly 96 in year one; the screen a doctor sees is a list, and a list of 96 is a different object from a list of 3. At Divyanka, standing orders per active buyer reach 3.4 by month nine — large enough to need sorting and staleness rules, not large enough to need search. The claim is testable and the answer changes the design.

Claim 3: the default is costly to reverse. At Diptanshu, reversing a template migration after clinicians have signed summaries against the new template is not a database operation; it is a documentation-integrity problem. At Divyanka, reversing an auto-created standing order after goods have shipped means physical returns from Tiruppur to Hubballi. Where reversal is genuinely cheap, the discipline still helps but stops being urgent.

Claim 4: the populations differ in inventory, not merely in tenure. This is the claim that distinguishes real narrative work from ceremony. Two cohorts that differ only in how long they have been customers do not need separate narratives. Two cohorts that differ in what they hold — one has templates, one does not — always do.

The discipline is actively misleading in three situations. First, when the interaction is genuinely one-shot — a first-time KYC verification, a single tax filing — writing a Day N narrative manufactures requirements for a state that never arrives. Second, when narrative is used as evidence of demand: three vivid stories about a feature nobody has asked for produce a well-specified product with no market, and the vividness makes the error harder to spot in review. Third, when the consumer of the feature is a machine. Divyanka's seller-side ERP integration has no Day 0 in the human sense; its analogue is schema versioning and backward compatibility, and dressing that up as a story about a person in a story about Tiruppur obscures the actual requirement, which is that version 1 clients must keep working for eighteen months.

5 · Hard edge cases

Multi-product estates. When a company sells several products to the same customer, a person can be at Day 0 on product B and Day N on product A, and they will carry product A's conventions into product B as expectations. Diptanshu sells an outpatient module and an inpatient module; a doctor who has used outpatient for three years arrives at the new inpatient assistant knowing exactly where the “sign” button sits — and if it has moved, the Day 0 narrative written for a naive user actively misdescribes her.

Two-sided markets. Every narrative doubles, and the two sides are never at the same maturity. Worse, the sides are coupled: the seller's Day N depends on how many buyers reached Day 1. Divyanka's honest position in February was that the seller narrative could not be written yet, because its content was a function of a buyer adoption rate nobody could forecast within a factor of two. The expert move there is not to write a fictional seller narrative but to write the seller narrative conditionally, at three levels of buyer adoption, and to specify what the seller sees at the lowest one.

Regulated products. Regulation adds narratives that have no commercial equivalent. Diptanshu had to write an amendment narrative — what happens when a signed discharge summary is found to be wrong — because a clinical record is append-only and correcting it means issuing an addendum with an audit trail, not editing a field. It had to write a consent narrative, because India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 does not permit a purpose to be quietly extended over data already collected, and using historical encounter notes to train or condition a drafting model is a new purpose. And it had to write a Day 1 narrative for the hospital's medical records officer, an actor who never appears in any product demo and who can stop a rollout single-handedly.

Hardware plus software. Diptesh Devices, a Coimbatore manufacturer of connected weighing scales used by kirana stores and small wholesalers, illustrates the hardest version. Its installed base is not one population but a fleet on mixed firmware, and Day 1 is per cohort. Atoms do not roll back: a change that alters a displayed weight cannot be undone by a deploy, because the shopkeeper has already sold at that weight, and re-verification of a weighing instrument is a physical visit governed by legal metrology rules.

AI-native products. Two peculiarities compound. The first is the trust decay already quantified. The second is that the product changes without the user doing anything: a model update alters Day N behaviour for people who made no choice and received no announcement. This breaks the usual assumption that state changes are caused by the user. The disciplined response is a version-stamped narrative — the specification states which model version the Day N account assumes, and a model change triggers a re-read of the Day N narrative in the same way a schema change triggers a migration review.

At the organisational seams, ownership is the real problem. Day 0 belongs to growth or onboarding. Day 1 belongs to whoever is shipping. Day N belongs to nobody, because by the time it arrives the squad has been re-formed and the Day-N symptoms present as support volume rather than as product defects. What mature companies say they do is write three narratives per feature. What they actually do, reliably, is run a launch-readiness review that forces the Day 1 question, and fund the Day N question eighteen months later out of an incident budget. The organisations that genuinely close this loop do one specific thing: they put a dated calendar item on the PRD itself — a Day N review at a stated accumulation threshold, not a stated date — and give it to the same person who wrote the document.

6 · Nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The default is written in passive voice

The tell is grammatical. Competent PRDs say “existing templates will be migrated to the new format.” An expert reads that sentence and asks who decided, what happens to the ones that fail, and what the clinician sees at 8 a.m. The obvious reading — that migration is an implementation detail — is wrong because the default determines the experience of ninety-five per cent of the population while occupying one line of a document nobody reviews.

Day N is a volume, not a date

The tell is a Day N section containing no number. An expert asks what grows and at what rate, then designs the screen for the ninetieth-percentile value rather than the mean. The obvious reading — “we'll see how it goes and iterate” — is wrong because the architecture decisions that make the ninetieth-percentile case survivable, such as whether goals or standing orders can be archived at all, are made at build time and are expensive afterwards.

Migration accuracy is the wrong metric; asymmetry is the right one

The tell is a team quoting a single accuracy figure. An expert asks for the confusion matrix and then asks which cell hurts. At Diptanshu, a template migration that made a summary more verbose was harmless; one that dropped a medication-reconciliation section was not. The obvious reading — higher accuracy is better — is wrong because effort spent moving 92 to 95 per cent overall is usually worth less than effort spent driving one dangerous error class to zero.

The fourth cell exists and nobody owns it

The tell is a returning user shown an onboarding tour for a feature they used eighteen months ago, or an inherited record whose owner has left the company. An expert writes a Day R narrative explicitly. The obvious reading — that returners are just existing users — is wrong because their expectations are stale, which is a different failure from having no expectations at all, and it produces support contacts that are hard to diagnose because the user is describing a product that used to exist.

Announcement reach caps everything else

The tell is a release note drafted after code freeze by someone who did not read the PRD. An expert specifies the announcement as a slot in the Day 1 narrative, with its own reach estimate. The obvious reading — that comms is a downstream activity — is wrong because a Day 1 narrative that thirty per cent of the base never enters is a specification of an experience thirty per cent of people have.

Narratives specify shape, not demand

The tell is a PRD that cites its own narrative as justification for building the feature. An expert keeps the evidence section and the narrative section visibly separate, and can state which research each claim in the narrative rests on. The obvious reading — that a compelling story indicates a real need — is wrong in a specific and dangerous way: narrative quality correlates with the writer's skill, not with the customer's willingness to act.

On marketplaces, one side's Day 0 is a function of the other side's Day 1

The tell is a seller narrative containing an order whose origin the document never explains. An expert writes the supply-side narrative at the lowest plausible demand level and checks that it is still tolerable. The obvious reading — write the seller story as it will look once the flywheel turns — is wrong because it specifies a state that occurs only after the risky period the specification was supposed to help you survive.

Assistive features specify what the human stops doing

The tell is a team celebrating a falling edit rate. An expert treats a falling intervention rate as an ambiguous signal requiring a separate measurement of outcome quality. The obvious reading — less editing means better drafts — is wrong whenever the human is the last line of defence, which in regulated products is almost always.

Reversibility is the design variable, not accuracy

The tell is a long argument about a model or heuristic's precision with no discussion of undo. An expert asks first where on the reversibility ladder the feature will sit, because that choice sets the accuracy bar rather than the other way round. The obvious reading — build the best classifier you can, then decide — is wrong because the ladder rung changes what you need to build, and deciding it late wastes the engineering.

A narrative that cannot be false is decoration

The tell is sentences about wanting, feeling and needing. An expert's narratives are full of checkable nouns: 41 orders in 14 months, 900-piece weekly capacity, 96 discharges a year. The obvious reading — that emotional texture makes a scenario persuasive — is wrong for specification purposes, though it remains true for persuasion, which is exactly why the two get confused.

7 · How this differs across product types and stages

In consumer products the greenfield population renews continuously, so Day 0 carries genuine weight; but even there the brownfield spike at launch is usually the single largest event, and consumer teams under-invest in it because their instincts are tuned to acquisition. In business and enterprise software the weighting inverts hard: new logos arrive a few a week, the installed base is the business, and Day 1 splits into three actors — the administrator who must enable, the manager whose reports change, and the frontline user who was not consulted. A feature loved by the frontline and invisible to the administrator does not get switched on, which is a specification failure and not an adoption failure.

In platforms and marketplaces everything doubles and couples, as Section 5 described. In hardware the cohort structure is physical and irreversible. In AI products the distinctive property is that Day N moves without the user, and that the human's vigilance is itself a component that degrades.

Where the difference is not real is worth saying plainly, because a great deal of writing on this topic invents distinctions. The six slots are the same in every product type. The four populations are the same. What changes is only the weights — the P, f and c of Exhibit 2 — and occasionally the addition of a regulated narrative such as amendment or consent. A practitioner who has internalised the grid does not need a different method for marketplaces; they need different numbers.

By stage, the honest statement is that early companies have almost no brownfield — with four thousand users you can email all of them, and migration is a spreadsheet — so Day 0 genuinely dominates, and the discipline can be applied lightly. The expensive error is continuing to specify like a startup long after the installed base has become the business. Divyanka crossed that line somewhere in 2024; its PRD template still had one narrative slot in 2026.

8 · Three worked examples

Example one: Diptanshu’s 641 templates

The migration classifier mapped each legacy template to one of eleven canonical structures. On a hand-labelled sample of 180 templates it was 89 per cent accurate. Applied automatically across 641 templates in 34 hospitals, it would have mis-mapped about 71 templates. Those templates were not equally weighted: the top 40 templates covered 78 per cent of discharge volume, and the classifier's accuracy on those was 96 per cent, because they were the most standard. The long tail — specialty templates in paediatric oncology, obstetrics and transplant units — was where errors clustered, and those were precisely the units where a dropped section carried clinical weight. Volume-weighted accuracy was 95 per cent; risk-weighted accuracy was closer to 74 per cent. Anand's decision followed from the second number, not the first: automatic migration for the top 40, and a review queue for the remaining 601 templates, worked by hospital medical records officers over six weeks before go-live.

Example two: Divyanka’s conditional seller narrative

Simran wrote the seller narrative three times, at 2, 8 and 20 per cent buyer adoption. At 2 per cent, a typical Tiruppur seller with 40 active buyers would see 0.8 standing orders — effectively an empty screen. At 8 per cent, 3.2 standing orders covering roughly 190 pieces a fortnight against 1,800 pieces of capacity: visible but not yet decision-relevant. At 20 per cent, 8 standing orders and 470 pieces, which is the level at which a seller would actually change a production plan. The specification therefore said something the original had not: until sellers see a median of five standing orders, the Standing Orders tab must not be the primary seller surface, and the announcement to sellers must be held. That single sentence saved the launch from teaching 4,100 manufacturers that the feature was empty.

Example three: how Diptesh Devices got it wrong, and what recovery cost

In 2024 Diptesh shipped an auto-tare feature to its connected scales — the scale would automatically subtract the weight of a known container. The specification was a clean Day 0 narrative about a shopkeeper unboxing a new scale. At the time 31,400 units had been sold and 22,600 were reporting; 61 per cent ran firmware 2.x, 34 per cent ran 1.9, and 5 per cent — about 1,130 units — ran 1.7, which used a different calibration constant. Auto-tare was enabled by default on all of them. On the 1.7 cohort the constant mismatch produced displayed weights up to 40 grams light. Shopkeepers under-charged, some customers noticed, and because a retail weighing instrument is a legally verified device, correcting it required a physical re-verification visit rather than a firmware push.

The recovery ran nine weeks: 1,130 field visits at an all-in cost of about ₹1,850 each, or ₹20.9 lakh, plus a 4.1-point drop in the company's dealer net promoter score that took two quarters to return. The specification change afterwards was small and permanent. Every Diptesh PRD now carries a firmware cohort table with counts, and no default may be enabled for a cohort that has not been named in a narrative. The lesson generalises past hardware: the failure was not a bad decision about auto-tare, it was that the document contained no population in which the decision could be seen to be wrong.

10 · Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether Day N can be specified in advance. The case for specifying it: the steady state is where a product spends nearly all of its life; the decisions that make it survivable — archiving, staleness, sorting, permissions, deletion semantics — are architectural and expensive to retrofit; and teams that defer it reliably never fund it, because Day N symptoms arrive as support volume rather than as defects. The case against: the accumulation variable's distribution is genuinely unknown before launch, Day N specifications written in advance are usually wrong in ways that generate real engineering cost, and the discipline of shipping something small and observing it is a better instrument than forecasting. This position would be wrong if it turned out that the expensive Day N decisions were cheap to change later; its holders point to products that shipped thin and adapted fine. Its opponents point to products where “we'll add archiving later” meant three years of unusable lists. The evidence is anecdotal on both sides and the disagreement is live.

Narrative versus enumeration for high-consequence flows. Cockburn's tradition holds that prose scenarios cannot be checked for completeness: you cannot tell, by reading, which exception flows are missing. In a clinical product this is a serious objection, and Diptanshu's quality team pressed it. The narrative school's steelman is that enumerated use-case documents achieve formal completeness and practical blindness — forty pages nobody reads closely, in which an absent flow is as invisible as it is in prose, and in which the situational detail that reveals a missing case has been stripped out. The synthesis people reach for — “narratives plus a checklist of exception classes” — is real practice, but it is a compromise rather than a resolution, and neither camp thinks it fully answers the other.

Whether brownfield should converge on greenfield. One school holds that every existing user should eventually be moved to the new experience, because carrying two experiences doubles the test matrix, confuses support, and guarantees that half the base is on the worse one. The other holds that grandfathering is a legitimate permanent product decision: the cost of a forced migration is paid in churn and trust by people who have already bought, and enterprise customers in particular are paying partly for stability. Divyanka faced this in a mild form and Diptanshu in an acute one — the hospitals with accreditation-approved template language had a defensible claim to keep it indefinitely. The disagreement resolves differently by contract structure, which is a hint that it is not really a design question at all.

Whether personas help. Cooper's position is that a named persona prevents the scenario from drifting to whoever is loudest in the room. The counter-position, common among data-led teams, is that personas launder an assumption as a person: “Priya” acquires properties nobody measured, and those properties then function as requirements. The practical compromise is to require every property in a narrative to be traceable to a measurable population statistic, which most teams say they do and few do.

11 · What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes three narratives because the template has three slots. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They start from the population arithmetic rather than the story: before writing a word of scenario they know the sizes, frequencies and error costs, and they allocate pages accordingly, which usually means the greenfield story gets shorter. They treat the default as the most consequential sentence in the document and argue about it in the same meeting where scope is decided, not two weeks before launch. They decide the reversibility rung before the engineering approach, because that choice sets the accuracy requirement rather than following from it. And they schedule the Day N review against an accumulation threshold rather than a date — “when the median user holds twenty of these” — and own it personally, because they know that no reorganisation will assign it to anyone else.

There is a fifth, subtler behaviour. An expert can say out loud which parts of a narrative are evidence and which are invention, and does so unprompted in review. That habit is what keeps narrative from becoming the most persuasive form of guessing available to a product team.

12 · The decisions

Anand's decision, taken on 11 March, had three parts. The 40 highest-volume templates would be migrated automatically and the remaining 601 placed in a review queue worked by each hospital's medical records officer, on the risk-weighted rather than volume-weighted accuracy argument. The assistant would sit on the proposal-plus-confirm rung permanently, with no configuration option to auto-sign, which he expected to cost adoption and accepted. And the specification would carry a mandated Day N control: a monthly sampled audit of 200 signed summaries against the draft, reported to the clinical governance committee, with a stated threshold — if escaped material errors exceeded 15 per 1,000, the assistant's suggestions would be restricted to structure rather than clinical content until the number recovered. He was explicit that this made the product slower and that he could not prove it was necessary.

Simran's decision, taken on 24 February, was to ship Standing Orders to buyers only, with the seller-side surface and the seller announcement held until the median active seller had five standing orders. She wrote the conditional seller narrative at three adoption levels into the PRD so that the holding decision had a stated release condition rather than a vague one, and she added a Day N rule at launch rather than later: a standing order with two consecutive skipped cycles would be marked stale, drop out of the seller's committed-demand view, and prompt the buyer once. The scope she cut to pay for it was a forecasting chart the sales team had asked for.

Three questions in the style of a teaching note. First: Anand's audit threshold of 15 escaped errors per 1,000 is a number he chose without a benchmark, and it commits the company to degrading its own product under a condition it cannot fully control. Was committing to it in writing, before launch, courageous or reckless — and what would you have needed to know to decide? Second: Simran's holding decision protects seller trust at the cost of a quarter of seller-side learning. On a two-sided market, is it ever right to launch a feature to the side that will find it empty, simply to find out what they do? Third: both protagonists ended on the same rung of the reversibility ladder from entirely different reasoning. Is proposal-plus-confirm a genuine principle, or is it the rung teams choose when they have not done the work to justify either neighbour?

13 · Going deeper

PRD structure is the container these narratives live in; a template with one narrative slot will keep producing one-narrative products regardless of what its authors believe, so changing the template is usually the highest-leverage intervention available. Customer journey mapping supplies the raw material: a narrative is a journey with the new feature inserted and the irrelevant channels removed, and teams that map first write better Day 1 stories because they already know what the customer was doing before the feature existed. PM artefacts: one-pager, PRD, spec, strategy doc clarifies which document carries which decision, and in particular where the migration default belongs — it is a product decision and not a spec detail. Writing a one-pager matters because the exposure arithmetic of Exhibit 2 belongs at the top of the shortest document, where it can still change the shape of the work.

Acceptance criteria and error cases is the step that converts narratives from writing into specification; each narrative should terminate in testable conditions, and the exception classes are precisely what the enumeration school of Section 10 is right about. Telemetry requirements let you find out after launch which of your narratives was true, and without them the Day N review has nothing to read. Non-functional requirements is where the Day N accumulation variable becomes a performance and storage question — a list of 96 items and a list of 9,600 are different engineering problems. And release criteria and success metrics is where Simran's holding condition and Anand's audit threshold properly live: a narrative that specifies a state the product must not enter is only enforceable if the release process knows about it.

Munadi Technologies: Day 0, Day 30, Day N

Kochi, Sunday 15 November 2026

1Sunday night, Kakkanad

By twenty past ten on the night of Sunday 15 November 2026 the fifth floor of Munadi Technologies' office at Infopark, Kakkanad, was down to one lit room. Yogeshwari Gopalan, Vice-President, Product, had the pilot numbers open on one screen. On the other she had a document she had written in October and shown to nobody.

In the morning she owed Yesodharan Gothuruth, the founder and chief executive, a plan for Collections — the payment-reminder and UPI collection module that Munadi had released to new shops on Tuesday 30 June and had been migrating existing shops onto since Monday 21 September. On 15 September, from the stage of a retail-technology summit in Bengaluru, Gothuruth had told the room that every shop on Munadi would be on Collections by 31 December.

The pilot's Day-30 read had landed on 21 October (Exhibit 2). New shops took to Collections. The migrated shops, all with at least eleven months of ledger, did not, and a third of them were entering less into the app than before. The requirements document for Collections, circulated on 12 February, had carried three customer narratives: Day 0, Day 30, Day N. On 9 March the Day-N narrative had been cut to hold the June date. Gopalan had written that memo.

2Munadi Technologies, 2017–2026

Gothuruth and two colleagues registered Munadi Technologies Private Limited in Kochi in September 2017, two months after the Goods and Services Tax arrived and small retailers found they needed something that printed a compliant invoice. The first product was a billing app for kirana shops, priced below Tally and sold door to door in Thrissur and Palakkad. A credit ledger — Indian shopkeepers sell on trust and collect later — was added in 2019 and became the reason shops stayed. Munadi raised ₹46 crore in August 2021 and ₹210 crore in February 2025.

The decision that governs this Monday was taken on Monday 14 March 2022. Shops in low-connectivity markets were losing entries when the network dropped, and Munadi's answer was to write to the handset first and sync afterwards. Ledger customer records were keyed by an identifier the handset generated, and nothing was built on the server to decide when two such records were the same person. The engineer who designed it left in 2023. Exhibit 3 shows the duplicate rate since.

On Tuesday 8 November 2022 Munadi signed a master agreement with the Mannarkad Group, a Malayali-owned supermarket business in Dubai, now ninety-six outlets across the UAE and Oman. Serving it required a multi-store build, which was forked from the single-shop ledger rather than merged into it. In August 2025 engineering recorded a plan to merge the fork within two quarters; at 31 October 2026, six of the eleven ledger endpoints were still forked.

3The industry

Munadi sells into a crowded middle. Tally sits above it in accounting, Zoho Books beside it in the cloud, Vyapar and myBillBook under it on price, and Khatabook and OkCredit taught Indian shopkeepers that a digital credit ledger could be free. Little in the category is now differentiated by invoicing; retention is bought with the ledger and, increasingly, with collection.

That is where the regulated plumbing helps. UPI reaches the smallest shop, NPCI's AutoPay and collect-request rails let a merchant ask for money rather than wait for it. Compliance supplies the rest of the calendar: GSTR-3B by the twentieth of the following month, e-invoicing for registered businesses above ₹5 crore of turnover, and, since the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023, a duty to tell a shop's customers what is being done with their phone numbers. ONDC has made catalogue data portable.

The pressure on Munadi's customers comes from elsewhere. Quick commerce — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart — has taken the top-up basket out of the neighbourhood shop, and JioMart Partner and Udaan have changed how that shop buys. Munadi's own exposure is wider than India: the Gulf outlets of the Mannarkad Group, and a diaspora grocery pipeline in the United States that its New Jersey office has been building since 2024.

4What happened, and what has since turned out otherwise

Collections began as a research project. In January 2026 Yadavi Govindan, Munadi's principal designer, and two researchers visited thirty-one shops in Thrissur and Coimbatore and wrote up what collection day looked like. The requirements document that followed on 12 February carried three narratives — a shop that installed Munadi that morning, the same shop a month in, and a shop eighteen months in — and one sentence that the team quoted for months afterwards: the Day-N shop is the Day-0 shop with more rows.

On Monday 9 March, Gopalan, then Director of Product, circulated a trade-off memo to hold a 30 June release. It cut the Day-N narrative and the server-side identity reconciliation that hung off it, and recorded duplicate ledger records as a long-tail hygiene issue below 3 per cent. Collections reached general availability on 30 June for new installs only. Gopalan was appointed Vice-President, Product, on 1 April 2026.

Four dated facts now sit beside those beliefs. The identity estimate computed on Tuesday 3 November, from band rates observed on a sample drawn on Monday 5 October, puts the pooled duplicate rate at 12.4 per cent of estimated ledger customer records, and 14.8 per cent in the oldest tenure band (Exhibit 3). The Day-30 read of 21 October puts Collections activation at 50.0 per cent for the 4,200 migrated shops against 64.0 per cent for new installs, and 67.0 per cent of migrated shops at or above 80 per cent of their own pre-migration ledger volume (Exhibit 2). The pilot cohort's fourth week, which closed on Sunday 18 October, stood at 94 on the volume index (Exhibit 5). In-app support contacts across the base ran at 24.5 per thousand shops in July and 38.6 in October (Exhibit 4).

8The options as Gopalan sees them

By Sunday evening Gopalan had four lines written on the whiteboard, with Exhibit 6 Panel B beside them.

Option 1 — migrate the whole eligible base by 31 December. The 1,19,700 shops in Exhibit 1 not yet on Collections move to it, with de-duplication running after migration rather than before. Fifty-four engineer-weeks, ₹44.60 lakh, against the 30.6 available, so it requires a waiver of the freeze or capacity from outside the squad. It is the option aimed at the date Gothuruth gave in Bengaluru, and it leaves the handset-generated identifier scheme of March 2022 in place.

Option 2 — two tracks. New installs continue on Collections; the rest of the base stays on the old ledger with no end date announced. Eleven engineer-weeks now, ₹9.09 lakh, and six engineer-weeks a quarter, ₹4.96 lakh, to carry both code paths. The identity scheme is untouched.

Option 3 — the 4–10 month band. Its 27,400 shops move by 31 December; the 11–22 and 23–55 month bands are decided after the new year. Twenty-six engineer-weeks, ₹21.48 lakh. The identity scheme is untouched.

Option 4 — re-specify. Migration stops, Govindan's team writes the Day-N narrative from field work, and requirements are rewritten from it, with replanning after the freeze lifts on 4 January. Eight engineer-weeks now, ₹6.61 lakh. Nothing migrates in December.

9The deadline and the hard constraints

Gopalan's plan is due to Gothuruth on Monday 16 November. The board meets on Thursday 3 December, and the release freeze runs from Friday 18 December to Monday 4 January; it has been waived twice, in December 2023 and December 2025.

Between 16 November and 17 December there are twenty-four working days, or 4.8 weeks. The Collections squad is nine engineers, six in Bengaluru and three in Pune, which gives 43.2 engineer-weeks gross. Of these, 12.6 are committed to the e-invoice schema update scheduled for 1 January 2027 and to the DPDP consent notices that the mobile-number matching in Exhibit 3 requires, leaving 30.6. Work that waits for the board on 3 December has eleven working days to 17 December, or 19.8 engineer-weeks gross and 7.2 after the committed work.

Munadi held ₹118 crore of cash on 31 October against net burn of ₹7.3 crore a month, about sixteen months. The Mannarkad master agreement of 8 November 2022 runs to 31 March 2027 and carries ninety days' notice for convenience, with service credits of 5 per cent of the quarterly fee of ₹36 lakh, ₹1.80 lakh a month, for each month in which month-end tax reporting is unavailable. The group is ₹1.44 crore a year, 2.63 per cent of Exhibit 6 Panel A.

At a quarter to midnight Gopalan read Govindan's Berlin email again, and then the October document she had not sent. It described one shop in Thrissur on the eight hundred and ninety-sixth day of using Munadi, and what that shopkeeper would lose on the morning the app changed under her. Gopalan had written it as a narrative because that was the form the February document used and the March memo dropped. She did not know whether it was a requirement, an argument or an apology, and she had until nine o'clock to decide which of the four lines on the whiteboard it belonged to.

10Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, describe the shop at each of the four tenure bands. Which band would you write a Day-N narrative for, and what do you give up by choosing it?
  2. Exhibit 2 reports Day-30 activation at 64.0 per cent in Panel A and 50.0 in Panel B. What must you establish before treating the gap as an effect of migration?
  3. Exhibit 5 puts week four at 94 on the volume index; Exhibit 2 Panel B puts 67.0 per cent of shops at or above 80 per cent of their own baseline. Reconcile them, and say which belongs before the board on 3 December.
  4. Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 4 both count support contacts. Set out what each one measures, what neither measures, and what you would ask the support desk to produce before 3 December.
  5. The memo of 9 March cut one of three narratives to protect a launch date. Write the requirement a Day-N narrative would have produced, and name the figures on this page Munadi would then have measured before 30 June.
  6. What should Gopalan do on Monday morning, 16 November, and what should she say to the board on 3 December about the 31 December commitment, the Mannarkad agreement and the 30.6 engineer-weeks?
